title: 👁️ IELTS Reading: The Smart Approach

sections.heading: The big mistake
sections.body: Most students read the whole passage first, then answer questions. This wastes 10–15 minutes and often causes panic.

sections.heading: The smart strategy
sections.body:
Step 1: Skim the passage (60 sec) — read first/last sentences of each paragraph only
Step 2: Read ALL the questions carefully
Step 3: Scan for specific answers — use keywords from questions

sections.heading: Key insight
sections.body: You don't need to understand every word. You need to locate information efficiently.

highlight: Questions follow the order of the passage (mostly). Work through the passage from top to bottom.

label: 📖 Read carefully — questions follow
text:
Urban farming — the practice of growing food within city boundaries — has gained significant attention as a potential solution to food security challenges. Proponents argue that urban agriculture can reduce food miles, improve nutritional access in low-income areas, and strengthen community bonds. Critics, however, point to the limited scale achievable within urban environments and question whether the yields justify the investment required.

Research from the University of Sheffield found that if all suitable urban surfaces in the UK were used for food production, they could supply vegetables for 15% of the population. While this figure is modest, supporters contend that urban farming's value extends beyond mere caloric contribution — it provides educational opportunities, green spaces, and mental health benefits that are difficult to quantify economically.
tip: Skim: paragraph 1 = arguments for/against urban farming. Paragraph 2 = research findings.

title: 🔍 Strategy: Locating Evidence
body:
For every question, ask: 'Which paragraph addresses this topic?'

Paragraph 1 topics: food security, food miles, nutrition, community, scale, investment
Paragraph 2 topics: research, UK statistics, scale, educational/mental health benefits

Once you know which paragraph to look in, scan for keywords — not exact phrase matches.

quick.label: Map topics to paragraphs BEFORE answering

statement: Urban farming has attracted attention as a solution to food security problems.
passage:
Urban farming — the practice of growing food within city boundaries — has gained significant attention as a potential solution to food security challenges. Proponents argue that urban agriculture can reduce food miles, improve nutritional access in low-income areas, and strengthen community bonds. Critics, however, point to the limited scale achievable within urban environments and question whether the yields justify the investment required.

Research from the University of Sheffield found that if all suitable urban surfaces in the UK were used for food production, they could supply vegetables for 15% of the population. While this figure is modest, supporters contend that urban farming's value extends beyond mere caloric contribution — it provides educational opportunities, green spaces, and mental health benefits that are difficult to quantify economically.
explanation: 'urban farming — the practice of growing food within city boundaries — has gained significant attention as a potential solution to food security challenges' — directly confirms the statement.

statement: The University of Sheffield research showed that urban farming could feed the entire UK population.
passage:
Urban farming — the practice of growing food within city boundaries — has gained significant attention as a potential solution to food security challenges. Proponents argue that urban agriculture can reduce food miles, improve nutritional access in low-income areas, and strengthen community bonds. Critics, however, point to the limited scale achievable within urban environments and question whether the yields justify the investment required.

Research from the University of Sheffield found that if all suitable urban surfaces in the UK were used for food production, they could supply vegetables for 15% of the population. While this figure is modest, supporters contend that urban farming's value extends beyond mere caloric contribution — it provides educational opportunities, green spaces, and mental health benefits that are difficult to quantify economically.
explanation:
The passage says '15% of the population' — not the ENTIRE population. The statement uses 'entire' which directly contradicts '15%'.

FALSE = passage says the OPPOSITE. Here, 'entire' contradicts '15%'.

statement: The mental health benefits of urban farming can be measured in precise economic terms.
passage:
Urban farming — the practice of growing food within city boundaries — has gained significant attention as a potential solution to food security challenges. Proponents argue that urban agriculture can reduce food miles, improve nutritional access in low-income areas, and strengthen community bonds. Critics, however, point to the limited scale achievable within urban environments and question whether the yields justify the investment required.

Research from the University of Sheffield found that if all suitable urban surfaces in the UK were used for food production, they could supply vegetables for 15% of the population. While this figure is modest, supporters contend that urban farming's value extends beyond mere caloric contribution — it provides educational opportunities, green spaces, and mental health benefits that are difficult to quantify economically.
explanation:
'mental health benefits that are difficult to quantify economically' — the passage says these benefits are DIFFICULT to quantify, meaning they CANNOT be measured precisely.

The statement says they 'can be measured in precise economic terms' — directly contradicted.

question: According to the passage, what do critics of urban farming argue?
options: The scale is too limited relative to the investment required
It is only suitable for wealthy areas
correct: The scale is too limited relative to the investment required
explanation:
'Critics, however, point to the limited scale achievable within urban environments and question whether the yields justify the investment required.'

Two criticisms: (1) limited scale, (2) yields don't justify investment.

The option 'scale is too limited relative to investment required' captures BOTH criticisms in one phrase.

question: What is the PURPOSE of the statistic '15% of the population' in the passage?
options: To prove urban farming is ineffective
To demonstrate the full potential of urban farming globally
To illustrate the modest but non-trivial contribution urban farming could make in the UK
To show that critics of urban farming are wrong
correct: To illustrate the modest but non-trivial contribution urban farming could make in the UK
explanation:
The author uses '15%' to:
✅ Acknowledge it is 'modest' (concedes the critics' point about scale)
✅ But then argues value 'extends beyond mere caloric contribution' (supports urban farming)

The statistic serves a CONCESSIVE function — it acknowledges a limitation while introducing a rebuttal.

This is a Band 8 inference question — you must understand WHY the author cites the data, not just what it says.
